data.text/markdown:
3D poses in SE(3)

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to work with rigid-body poses in 3D: a translation plus a rotation. It shows:
  • How one rotation is written as yaw, pitch and roll angles, as a rotation matrix, and as a unit quaternion (CPose3D, CPose3DQuat, CQuaternionDouble).
  • Pose composition ||(\oplus||), inverse composition ||(\ominus||) and the inverse, to chain coordinate frames (robot, camera, observed point).
  • Smooth interpolation between keyframe poses (CPose3DInterpolator).
All of it lives in the mrpt.poses and mrpt.math modules. Move the sliders to change the robot pose; the 3D views (drag to rotate them) and all numbers update. Try a pitch of ±90° to meet gimbal lock.

data.text/html: Robot pose (in the world frame)

data.text/markdown:
1. One rotation, three representations

MRPT uses the yaw-pitch-roll (Z-Y-X) convention: the rotation matrix is ||(R = R_z(\text{yaw})\, R_y(\text{pitch})\, R_x(\text{roll})||). Its columns are the robot's own x, y, z axes, expressed in the world frame. A unit quaternion ||(q = (q_r, q_x, q_y, q_z)||) encodes the same rotation with four numbers and no singularities (||(q||) and ||(-q||) are the same rotation). The homogeneous matrix stacks ||(R||) and the translation ||(t||), so that a point maps as ||(p_{world} = R\, p_{robot} + t||).

data.text/markdown:
2. Chaining frames: composition and inverse

A camera is mounted on the robot, 0.5 m ahead and 0.8 m up, tilted 20° down. That mounting pose ||(B||) is given in the robot frame, so the camera pose in the world is the composition ||(A \oplus B||) of the robot pose ||(A||) and ||(B||). The camera sees a point 2.5 m ahead, along its own x axis. The inverse composition undoes it: ||((A \oplus B) \ominus A = B||), where ||(C \ominus A = A^{-1} \oplus C||) is "the pose of ||(C||) as seen from ||(A||)". With the identity pose ||(I||), ||(I \ominus A||) is just the inverse ||(A^{-1}||).

data.text/markdown:
3. Interpolating between poses

Keyframe poses at known times are a common way to describe a trajectory. CPose3DInterpolator returns the pose at any time in between: linear interpolation for the translation and SLERP (spherical linear interpolation of quaternions) for the rotation, which turns at constant rate along the shortest arc. Here the keyframes are the world origin (||(t = 0||) s), the robot pose ||(A||) (||(t = 1||) s), and ||(A||) followed by a fixed motion (||(t = 2||) s).
